summary.text: 上 works like a positional sign: a short mark placed above a reference line indicates the upper side or “above.” Early accounts differ over whether the line was curved or horizontal. The dossier’s reported inscriptional examples include Shang-period 上帝 and 上甲.

formation.text: Indicative (指事): the graph marks a position above a reference line. The received Shuowen analysis also classifies it as indicative, but records a Han-era interpretation rather than proof of the earlier graphic history.

history.text: Paleographic accounts describe the early graph as a short mark above a longer baseline; they disagree over whether early examples had a curved baseline or two horizontal strokes. Later forms altered the upper mark, with many accounts describing it as vertical to distinguish 上 from 二; the modern standard form is described as adding a dot. These are graphic changes, not evidence of a change in meaning.

The received Shuowen text treats 丄 as an ancient form meaning “high” and 上 as its seal-script form. A separate record notes an editorial difference over whether the received Shuowen head form is 丄 or 二; these are records of the lexicographic tradition, not independent confirmation of Shang graph history.

uncertainties.text: The dossier’s earliest discussed graph is oracle-bone 上, but it establishes no earlier dated occurrence. The inscriptional examples and dates are reported mainly by paleographic dictionaries rather than verified directly against the named artifacts; one artifact transcription includes 上甲 without isolating the character in its photograph.
The accounts agree on a mark above a reference line but differ on the line’s early shape. No primary inscription image in this dossier resolves whether it was curved or horizontal.

The dossier reports spatial “above/upper side,” “at/on the side of,” “more than,” authority-related uses, and the verbs “ascend” and “send up,” but does not establish a dated sequence linking these meanings. The graph’s construction is supported independently of that unresolved semantic chronology.

senses.period: Shang oracle-bone and Zhou bronze inscription contexts reported
senses.text: Paleographic accounts report Shang-period uses including 上帝, 上甲, and contrasts with 下; Zhou bronze examples include spatial “above.” These reports support early spatial uses, without establishing priority among every lexical use.
A paleographic account reports this spatial use in Zhou bronze examples. The dossier does not establish whether it developed from “above” or represents a distinct contextual use.
A paleographic account reports 上 in a tally where 以上 means “more than”; this compound example does not by itself establish a single-character sense or its development from “above.”

senses.gloss: ruler, elder, or person in authority
senses.text: Later literary uses with authority-related meanings are reported, but their precise chronology and semantic connection to the spatial sense are not established here.
The supplied phonological rows distinguish a verb glossed “ascend” from the noun “top, above.” The dossier does not establish when the verbal use arose or a semantic path connecting the two.
The supplied phonological rows include a verb glossed “to put up.” The dossier does not establish its chronology or development from the spatial sense.
Current dictionary metadata gives spatial, rank-related, and upward-action glosses. The list does not establish their historical sequence.

limitations.text: The dossier supports early spatial uses and reports several other uses, but does not establish dated semantic transitions among them. Compounds such as 上帝, 上甲, and 以上 are contextual examples, not automatically independent senses of 上.
The local reconstructed phonological rows are separate lexical entries for “ascend,” “put up,” and “top, above”; their readings do not establish semantic chronology or graphic origin.

overview.text: A small mark above a reference line indicates “above” or the upper side. The early line is described either as curved or horizontal; the graph’s basic positional construction is shared across these accounts.
